claim: The adult cephalopod mollusk Octopus vulgaris has a highly centralized brain containing about 200 million nerve cells in the supra- and subesophageal mass and two optic lobes.
source: The adult cephalopod mollusk Octopus vulgaris has a highly centralized brain containing about 200 million nerve cells in the supra- and subesophageal mass and two optic lobes (Young, 1963; Young, 1971), yet the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving brain development remain poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to Young, 1963 and Young, 1971

claim: At hatching, the O. vulgaris brain counts about 200,000 cells and occupies roughly one fourth of the total body.
source: At hatching, the O. vulgaris brain counts about 200,000 cells and occupies roughly one fourth of the total body, indicating extensive embryonic neurogenesis (Budelmann, 1995; Giuditta et al., 1971; Packard and Albergoni, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citations to Budelmann, 1995; Giuditta et al., 1971; Packard and Albergoni, 1970

claim: At hatching, the O. vulgaris brain indicates extensive embryonic neurogenesis.
source: At hatching, the O. vulgaris brain counts about 200,000 cells and occupies roughly one fourth of the total body, indicating extensive embryonic neurogenesis (Budelmann, 1995; Giuditta et al., 1971; Packard and Albergoni, 1970).
evidence: Inference based on the large number of cells and brain size at hatching, supported by citations

claim: In clades harboring species with diffuse nerve nets such as cnidaria and hemichordates, the proliferating neural progenitor cells are distributed throughout the ectoderm generating local neurons.
source: In clades harboring species with diffuse nerve nets such as cnidaria and hemichordates, the proliferating neural progenitor cells are distributed throughout the ectoderm generating local neurons, while in (sub)phyla with a centralized nervous system including vertebrates, arthropods and some annelids, the neural progenitor cells are grouped in the neurectoderm.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about neural development across taxa

claim: In (sub)phyla with a centralized nervous system including vertebrates, arthropods and some annelids, the neural progenitor cells are grouped in the neurectoderm.
source: In clades harboring species with diffuse nerve nets such as cnidaria and hemichordates, the proliferating neural progenitor cells are distributed throughout the ectoderm generating local neurons, while in (sub)phyla with a centralized nervous system including vertebrates, arthropods and some annelids, the neural progenitor cells are grouped in the neurectoderm.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about neural development across taxa

claim: The proliferating neural progenitor cells either remain on the apical surface of the neurectoderm in vertebrates and annelids, or internalize as is the case for insects.
source: The proliferating neural progenitor cells either remain on the apical surface of the neurectoderm in vertebrates and annelids, or internalize as is the case for insects (Cunningham and Casey, 2014; Götz and Huttner, 2005; Hartenstein and Stollewerk, 2015; Lowe et al., 2003; Meyer and Seaver, 2009; Rentzsch et al., 2017; Simionato et al., 2008; Taverna et al., 2014; Urbach and Technau, 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to comparative developmental biology studies

claim: Long-distance migration of neurons has been described for developing vertebrate brains, in which neurons born in different zones follow long trajectories to their final location, where they intermingle to form complex circuits.
source: In addition, long-distance migration of neurons has been described for developing vertebrate brains, in which neurons born in different zones follow long trajectories to their final location, where they intermingle to form complex circuits (García-Moreno and Molnár, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to García-Moreno and Molnár, 2020

claim: Neuronal migration in developing invertebrate nervous systems is generally limited to restricted cell populations or to short-range migratory events.
source: Although neuronal migration has been described in developing invertebrate nervous systems as well, this process is generally limited to restricted cell populations, for example the Q, CAN and HSN neuroblasts in Caenorhabditis elegans (Blelloch et al., 1999; Forrester et al., 1998; Montell, 1999), or to short-range migratory events, for example in the Drosophila visual system (Apitz and Salecker, 2015; Bhat, 2007; Morante et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in C. elegans and Drosophila

claim: Group B SRY-related HMG box genes (soxB genes) regulate the generation of the neurectoderm and also maintain neurectodermal cells in an undifferentiated and proliferative state.
source: First, group B SRY-related HMG box genes (soxB genes) regulate the generation of the neurectoderm and also maintain neurectodermal cells in an undifferentiated and proliferative state (Guth and Wegner, 2008; Sarkar and Hochedlinger, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guth and Wegner, 2008; Sarkar and Hochedlinger, 2013

claim: Members of the superfamily of basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors control the specification of neural progenitor cells and also activate neuronal differentiation pathways.
source: After neurectoderm formation, members of the superfamily of basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors control the specification of neural progenitor cells and also activate neuronal differentiation pathways (Bertrand et al., 2002; Vervoort and Ledent, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertrand et al., 2002; Vervoort and Ledent, 2001

claim: bHLH genes such as atonal, neurogenic differentiation (neuroD) and neurogenin (ngn), and achaete-scute (asc) complex members are classified in group A.
source: bHLH genes such as atonal, neurogenic differentiation (neuroD) and neurogenin (ngn), and achaete-scute (asc) complex members are classified in group A.
evidence: Draws from established classification of bHLH transcription factors

claim: Members of bHLH group A regulate the patterning, differentiation and specification of neurons, from sponges to primates.
source: The role of bHLH genes is best described in nervous system development where members of this group A (and some of group B) regulate the patterning, differentiation and specification of neurons, from sponges to primates (Powell and Jarman, 2008; Simionato et al., 2007; Vervoort and Ledent, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Powell and Jarman, 2008; Simionato et al., 2007; Vervoort and Ledent, 2001

claim: Regulatory genes such as musashi, prospero, and embryonic lethal abnormal vision (elav) activate programs to initiate differentiation of progenitor cells into neurons.
source: After this neural progenitor commitment, regulatory genes such as musashi, prospero, and embryonic lethal abnormal vision (elav) (vertebrate hu), will activate programs to initiate differentiation of progenitor cells into neurons (Choksi et al., 2006; Okano et al., 2002; Pascale et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Choksi et al., 2006; Okano et al., 2002; Pascale et al., 2008

claim: One lineage tracing study in the squid Doryteuthis pealeii revealed that cells surrounding the eye placode contribute to the anterior chamber organ, the supraesophageal mass, the buccal mass and the buccal ganglion.
source: One lineage tracing study in the squid Doryteuthis pealeii revealed that cells surrounding the eye placode contribute to the anterior chamber organ, the supraesophageal mass, the buccal mass and the buccal ganglion (Koenig et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koenig et al., 2016

claim: O. vulgaris displays a direct embryonic development, giving rise to actively feeding paralarvae.
source: O. vulgaris displays a direct embryonic development, giving rise to actively feeding paralarvae.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about O. vulgaris development

claim: O. vulgaris embryonic development takes approximately 40 days at 19°C.
source: Their embryonic development takes approximately 40 days at 19°C and has been classified in 20 major stages I-XX, with some stages subdivided in an early and late part (Deryckere et al., 2020; Naef, 1928).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deryckere et al., 2020; Naef, 1928

claim: O. vulgaris embryonic development has been classified in 20 major stages I-XX, with some stages subdivided in an early and late part.
source: Their embryonic development takes approximately 40 days at 19°C and has been classified in 20 major stages I-XX, with some stages subdivided in an early and late part (Deryckere et al., 2020; Naef, 1928).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deryckere et al., 2020; Naef, 1928

claim: Organogenesis starts at Stage VII.2 in O. vulgaris.
source: Organogenesis starts at Stage VII.2 and can be split in early, mid-, and late phases (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: In the early organogenesis phase, the brain anlagen (cordal) are elongated and interconnected (in three dimensions).
source: In the early organogenesis phase, the brain anlagen (cordal) are elongated and interconnected (in three dimensions) (Figure 1A,B) as also described by Shigeno et al. for Octopus bimaculoides (Shigeno et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A,B and citation to Shigeno et al., 2015

claim: The cerebral cord (CC) will give rise to the lobes of the supraesophageal mass (SEM).
source: On the most anterior side, lateral and posterior to the mouth and foregut, the cerebral cord (CC) will give rise to the lobes of the supraesophageal mass (SEM), while on the posterior side of the embryo, the palliovisceral (PVC) and pedal (PC) cords will form the subesophageal mass (SUB).
evidence: Based on developmental observations and anatomical knowledge

claim: The palliovisceral (PVC) and pedal (PC) cords will form the subesophageal mass (SUB).
source: On the most anterior side, lateral and posterior to the mouth and foregut, the cerebral cord (CC) will give rise to the lobes of the supraesophageal mass (SEM), while on the posterior side of the embryo, the palliovisceral (PVC) and pedal (PC) cords will form the subesophageal mass (SUB).
evidence: Based on developmental observations and anatomical knowledge

claim: The two bilateral optic cords (OC) will differentiate and grow to form the optic lobes (OL).
source: The two bilateral optic cords (OC) will differentiate and grow to form the optic lobes (OL) (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A,C showing developmental progression

claim: At hatching, the central brain surrounds the esophagus and contains densely packed nuclei.
source: At hatching, the central brain that now surrounds the esophagus is considerably big and contains densely packed nuclei (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1D showing DAPI staining

claim: The tissue adjacent to the eye primordia first grows in size from Stage VII.2 to Stage XV.2, and then shrinks to disappear at hatching.
source: In contrast to the growing brain cords, the tissue adjacent to the eye primordia first grows in size from Stage VII.2 to Stage XV.2, and then shrinks to disappear at hatching, suggesting this tissue might contribute to the inner head structures (Figure 1A).
evidence: Observed in developmental series shown in Figure 1A

claim: The tissue adjacent to the eye primordia might contribute to the inner head structures.
source: In contrast to the growing brain cords, the tissue adjacent to the eye primordia first grows in size from Stage VII.2 to Stage XV.2, and then shrinks to disappear at hatching, suggesting this tissue might contribute to the inner head structures (Figure 1A).
evidence: Speculative inference based on the tissue's growth and disappearance pattern

claim: The tissue adjacent to the eye primordia was first described as 'Kopflappen' by Marquis.
source: This tissue was first described as 'Kopflappen' by Marquis and later as 'anterior chamber organ' by Koenig et al., 2016; Marquis, 1989; Shigeno et al., 2001; Yamamoto et al., 2003.
evidence: Supported by citation to Marquis, 1989

claim: The term 'anterior chamber organ' was introduced by Young, referring to neurovenous tissue adjacent to the adult eye.
source: However, the term 'anterior chamber organ' was introduced by Young, referring to neurovenous tissue adjacent to the adult eye, that presumably regulates the fluid content between the lens and cornea (Young, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citation to Young, 1970

claim: The structure adjacent to the eye is not restricted to the anterior side of each eye, but is rather placed lateral to the eye fields.
source: The term was most likely wrongly adopted embryonically as the tissue at that stage is not restricted to the anterior side of each eye, but is rather placed lateral to the eye fields.
evidence: Based on 3D imaging observations

claim: Based on 3D light sheet imaging, the structure adjacent to the eye is connected to the central brain through a stream-like transition zone.
source: Based on 3D light sheet imaging, we could clearly show that the structure is also connected to the central brain, through a stream-like transition zone.
evidence: Based on light sheet microscopy data

claim: The tissue adjacent to the eye was renamed to 'lateral lips' based on its position and shape.
source: Because of its position and shape, we renamed the tissue to 'lateral lips' (LL, indicated in mint green in Figure 1C,E) and introduced the terms 'anterior transition zone' (ATZ) and 'posterior transition zone' (PTZ) for the region that interconnects the lateral lips with the central brain on the anterior or posterior side of the embryo, respectively (Figure 1C,F).
evidence: Authors' nomenclature decision based on anatomical observations shown in Figure 1C,E,F

claim: Three candidate elav transcripts were identified in O. vulgaris.
source: Through blast searches against the full-length transcriptome of O. vulgaris embryos and paralarval brains generated in this study (see Materials and methods), we identified three candidate elav transcripts.
evidence: Based on transcriptome analysis performed in this study

claim: One of the O. vulgaris ELAV candidate proteins nested with vertebrate HuC/D and invertebrate neural ELAV homologs.
source: One of the O. vulgaris ELAV candidate proteins nested with vertebrate HuC/D and invertebrate neural ELAV homologs. We refer to this sequence as Ov-ELAV.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The two other ELAV candidate proteins could be identified as non-neural.
source: The two other candidate proteins could be identified as non-neural (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: An ELAV/HuD family splicing factor domain was detected in Ov-ELAV, which is characteristic of ELAV proteins.
source: We also performed a conserved domain (CD)-Search and detected an ELAV/HuD family splicing factor domain which is characteristic of ELAV proteins.
evidence: Based on conserved domain search analysis

claim: Ov-elav transcripts were detected throughout development with little expression at Stage IX in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal, and optic cords.
source: Ov-elav transcripts were detected throughout development with little expression at Stage IX in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal, and optic cords (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2A

claim: Strong Ov-elav staining was observed from Stage XI onwards, with low-level staining in the lateral lips and more intense staining in all cords and surrounding the mouth.
source: Strong staining was observed from Stage XI onwards, with low-level staining in the lateral lips surrounding the eye placode and more intense staining in all cords and surrounding the mouth (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2B

claim: At Stage XIII, a region in between the lateral lips and the central brain on the posterior side of the embryo showed intermediate Ov-elav expression, corresponding to the posterior transition zone (PTZ).
source: At Stage XIII, a region in between the lateral lips and the central brain on the posterior side of the embryo showed intermediate Ov-elav expression. This region corresponds to the posterior transition zone (PTZ), introduced earlier (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2C

claim: From Stage XV.2 onwards, cells on the anterior side of the embryo and laterally from the supraesophageal mass, corresponding to the anterior transition zone (ATZ), showed intermediate Ov-elav expression levels.
source: From Stage XV.2 onwards, cells on the anterior side of the embryo and laterally from the supraesophageal mass, corresponding to the anterior transition zone (ATZ), showed intermediate Ov-elav expression levels as well (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2D,E

claim: In the optic lobes at stages XIX.1 and XX.2, Ov-elav expression was highest in the medulla and inner granular layer, but lower in the outer granular layer.
source: In the optic lobes at stages XIX.1 and XX.2, Ov-elav expression was highest in the medulla and inner granular layer, but lower in the outer granular layer.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization observations

claim: The ATZ and PTZ shrink toward the end of embryonic development and seem to become integrated in the developing brain.
source: The ATZ and PTZ shrink toward the end of embryonic development and seem to become integrated in the developing brain (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Based on observations shown in Figure 2F,G

claim: Neuronal differentiation is present at early organogenesis phases in O. vulgaris.
source: In summary, our data indicate that neuronal differentiation is present at early organogenesis phases already, and the transition zones as well as the growing cords and masses contain large numbers of differentiating neurons.
evidence: Inference based on Ov-elav expression data

claim: The transition zones as well as the growing cords and masses contain large numbers of differentiating neurons.
source: In summary, our data indicate that neuronal differentiation is present at early organogenesis phases already, and the transition zones as well as the growing cords and masses contain large numbers of differentiating neurons.
evidence: Inference based on Ov-elav expression data

claim: Ov-syt was first detected in the retina at Stage XI.
source: In O. vulgaris, we observed expression of Ov-syt in the retina from Stage XI onwards (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2H,I

claim: Ov-syt was first expressed in the outer layers of the optic cord at Stage XIII.
source: In the central brain, it was first expressed in the outer layers of the optic cord at Stage XIII, and in the optic lobe medulla, supra- and subesophageal masses from Stage XV.2 onwards, pointing to a sequential maturation (Figure 2J–N).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2J-N

claim: Ov-syt was expressed in the optic lobe medulla, supra- and subesophageal masses from Stage XV.2 onwards, pointing to a sequential maturation.
source: In the central brain, it was first expressed in the outer layers of the optic cord at Stage XIII, and in the optic lobe medulla, supra- and subesophageal masses from Stage XV.2 onwards, pointing to a sequential maturation (Figure 2J–N).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2J-N; inference about sequential maturation

claim: First low-level immunoreactivity against acetylated alpha tubulin was found from Stage XV.2 onwards within the optic lobes.
source: First low-level immunoreactivity against acetylated alpha tubulin was found from Stage XV.2 onwards within the optic lobes (Figure 2O–U).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2O-U

claim: The embryonic cords demonstrate clear signs of differentiation from Stage XV.2 onwards.
source: We therefore used the adult terminology (optic lobe, supra- and subesophageal mass) for CNS annotation from this stage onwards, since the embryonic cords demonstrate clear signs of differentiation.
evidence: Inference based on Ov-syt expression and acetylated alpha-tubulin immunoreactivity

claim: PCNA is a nuclear protein required for DNA replication and repair, and functions as a cofactor of DNA polymerase-delta in eukaryotes and archaea.
source: PCNA is a nuclear protein required for DNA replication and repair, and functions as a cofactor of DNA polymerase-delta in eukaryotes and archaea (Barry and Bell, 2006; Baserga, 1991; Prelich et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barry and Bell, 2006; Baserga, 1991; Prelich et al., 1987

claim: Expression of pcna is tightly regulated and peaks at late G1 and S phases of the cell cycle.
source: Expression of pcna is tightly regulated and peaks at late G1 and S phases of the cell cycle (Santos et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santos et al., 2015

claim: Ov-pcna transcripts were detected throughout embryonic development.
source: Ov-pcna transcripts were detected throughout embryonic development (Figure 3A–D,I–L).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A-D,I-L

claim: At Stages VII.2 and IX, Ov-pcna transcripts were found in most embryonic tissues (mouth apparatus, retina, lateral lips and cords, in the latter at lower intensity).
source: While at Stages VII.2 and IX, transcripts were found in most embryonic tissues (mouth apparatus, retina, lateral lips and cords, in the latter at lower intensity), transcripts gradually disappeared in the optic, cerebral, palliovisceral and pedal cords from Stage XI onwards (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A-C

claim: Ov-pcna transcripts gradually disappeared in the optic, cerebral, palliovisceral and pedal cords from Stage XI onwards.
source: While at Stages VII.2 and IX, transcripts were found in most embryonic tissues (mouth apparatus, retina, lateral lips and cords, in the latter at lower intensity), transcripts gradually disappeared in the optic, cerebral, palliovisceral and pedal cords from Stage XI onwards (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A-C

claim: At Stage XI, most Ov-pcna expressing cells that were found adjacent to the eye, located to an area that is Ov-elav negative and that might be part of the epithelium lining the sinus ophthalmicus.
source: At Stage XI, most Ov-pcna expressing cells that were found adjacent to the eye, located to an area that is Ov-elav negative and that might be part of the epithelium lining the sinus ophthalmicus (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3C; speculation about tissue identity

claim: Ov-pcna transcripts were dispersed throughout the lateral lips and were absent from the transition zones and central brain at Stages XIII-XX.2.
source: Ov-pcna transcripts were dispersed throughout the lateral lips and were absent from the transition zones and central brain at Stages XIII-XX.2 (Figure 3D,I–L).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3D,I-L

claim: Histone H3 is phosphorylated on serine 10 and serine 28 during early mitosis and dephosphorylated at the end of mitosis in eukaryotes.
source: Histone H3 is phosphorylated on serine 10 and serine 28 during early mitosis and dephosphorylated at the end of mitosis in eukaryotes (Hans and Dimitrov, 2001; Prigent and Dimitrov, 2003; Wei et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hans and Dimitrov, 2001; Prigent and Dimitrov, 2003; Wei et al., 1998

claim: Mitotic activity in the embryonic head region was high at the beginning of organogenesis, with the highest level of dividing cells present in the mouth apparatus, at the apical side in the developing retina and spread throughout the lateral lips.
source: Immunohistochemistry on embryonic tissue from Stage VII.2 to XX.2 showed that mitotic activity in the embryonic head region was high at the beginning of organogenesis, with the highest level of dividing cells present in the mouth apparatus, at the apical side in the developing retina and spread throughout the lateral lips (Figure 3E–H,M–P).
evidence: Based on PH3 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3E-H,M-P

claim: The number of PH3-positive cells in the cerebral, optic, palliovisceral and pedal cords was limited, with possibly very few, single, dim and seemingly randomly organized positive cells present until Stage XIII.
source: Consistent with Ov-pcna expression, the number of PH3-positive cells in the cerebral, optic, palliovisceral and pedal cords was limited, with possibly very few, single, dim and seemingly randomly organized positive cells present until Stage XIII (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: Based on PH3 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3E-H

claim: At late organogenesis and maturation stages, PH3-positive cells located to the lateral lips and were absent from the central brain.
source: At late organogenesis and maturation stages, PH3-positive cells located to the lateral lips and were absent from the central brain (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: Based on PH3 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3M-P

claim: The lateral lips represent a major octopus neurogenic zone.
source: Given that the elav-positive areas are almost devoid of dividing cells, and the transition zone represents an area connecting the mitotically active lateral lips to the growing CNS, our data strongly suggest that the lateral lips represent a major octopus neurogenic zone.
evidence: Inference based on Ov-elav, Ov-pcna, and PH3 expression patterns

claim: O. vulgaris has single homologs for SOXC, D and E and two SOXB homologs.
source: Based on phylogenetic analysis including 31 SOXB, 3 SOXC, 4 SOXD, 4 SOXE, and 3 SOXF amino acid sequences from other species together with 5 TCF/LEF sequences to root the tree, we identified single O. vulgaris homologs for SOXC, D and E and two SOXB homologs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: One O. vulgaris SOXB protein nested within the SOXB2 clade and the other one within the SOXB1 clade.
source: One O. vulgaris SOXB protein nested within the SOXB2 clade and the other one within the SOXB1 clade, the latter named Ov-SOXB1.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: CD-Search of Ov-SOXB1 protein revealed the highly conserved SOX-TCF HMG-box and SOXp superfamily domains.
source: CD-Search of this Ov-SOXB1 protein revealed the highly conserved SOX-TCF HMG-box and SOXp superfamily domains.
evidence: Based on conserved domain search analysis

claim: Ov-soxB1 transcript levels were high in the head region at all embryonic stages examined.
source: Ov-soxB1 transcript levels were high in the head region at all embryonic stages examined (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: At Stage IX, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the lateral lips, eyes and surface ectoderm surrounding the mouth apparatus.
source: At Stage IX, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the lateral lips, eyes and surface ectoderm surrounding the mouth apparatus (esophagus, radula, salivary gland).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization observations

claim: At Stage IX, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the cerebral cord, but not in the palliovisceral, pedal and optic cords.
source: In the developing central brain, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the cerebral cord, but not in the palliovisceral, pedal and optic cords (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D

claim: At Stage XI, Ov-soxB1 was highly expressed in the lateral lips and cerebral cord, and transcripts were present in the optic cord in a patched pattern.
source: At Stage XI, Ov-soxB1 was still highly expressed in the lateral lips and cerebral cord, and transcripts were now also present in the optic cord in a patched pattern (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-H

claim: At Stage XIII, Ov-soxB1 transcripts were most highly expressed in the cerebral cord and showed a similar patched pattern in the optic cords, and were present in the pedal cord and limited in the palliovisceral cord.
source: At Stage XIII, Ov-soxB1 transcripts were most highly expressed in the cerebral cord and showed a similar patched pattern in the optic cords. Transcripts were also present in the pedal cord and limited in the palliovisceral cord (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I–L).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2I-L

claim: At Stage XV.2, Ov-soxB1 expression was high in the lateral lips and supraesophageal mass, spread in the subesophageal mass, and highest in the inner granular layer of the optic lobes.
source: At Stage XV.2, Ov-soxB1 expression was high in the lateral lips and supraesophageal mass. In the subesophageal mass, Ov-soxB1-positive cells were more spread and in the optic lobes, Ov-soxB1 transcripts showed the highest expression in the inner granular layer, while expression was more distributed in the outer granular layer and medulla (Figure 4—figure supplement 2M–P).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2M-P

claim: At Stages XIX.1 and XX.2, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the lateral lips, the supra- and subesophageal mass and optic lobes where it was most highly expressed in the inner granular layer.
source: At Stages XIX.1 and XX.2, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the lateral lips, the supra- and subesophageal mass and optic lobes where it was most highly expressed in the inner granular layer (Figure 4—figure supplement 2U-b).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2U-b

claim: Ov-soxB1 was not only expressed in putative stem cells, but also in postmitotic (Ov-elav+) areas.
source: Taken together, Ov-soxB1 was not only expressed in putative stem cells, but also in postmitotic (Ov-elav+) areas, as has been described for other invertebrate species.
evidence: Inference based on Ov-soxB1 and Ov-elav expression patterns; comparison to other species

claim: Phylogenetic analysis effectively assigned Ov-neuroD and Ov-ngn to their respective subfamilies.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the atonal-related bHLH transcription factors including 15 NEUROD and 8 NEUROGENIN/TAP protein sequences from other species effectively assigned Ov-neuroD and Ov-ngn to their respective subfamilies (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: CD-Search identified conserved bHLH domains in Ov-neuroD and Ov-ngn.
source: bHLH proteins possess a bHLH domain which is involved in DNA binding and dimerization (Jones, 2004; Murre et al., 1989). CD-Search identified such conserved domains in both sequences.
evidence: Based on conserved domain search analysis; supported by citations to Jones, 2004; Murre et al., 1989

claim: Phylogenetic analysis placed Ov-ASCL1 within the proneuronal ASCa subgroup of the bHLH superfamily.
source: In addition, phylogenetic analysis for the achaete-scute-related bHLH gene Ov-ascl1 together with 27 other ASCa protein sequences and 10 ASCb protein sequences placed Ov-ASCL1 within the proneuronal ASCa subgroup of the bHLH superfamily (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: CD-Search revealed a highly conserved DNA-binding bHLH domain in Ov-ASCL1.
source: CD-Search revealed a highly conserved DNA-binding bHLH domain.
evidence: Based on conserved domain search analysis

claim: Ov-ascl1 transcripts were detected throughout embryonic development at all stages tested.
source: In O. vulgaris, Ov-ascl1 transcripts were detected throughout embryonic development at all stages tested (Figure 4A–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4A-G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5

claim: At Stage IX, Ov-ascl1 was expressed in the lateral lips surrounding the eye primordia, in retinal cells of the developing eyes and in the tissue delineating the mouth apparatus, and was absent from the cerebral, pedal, palliovisceral and optic cords.
source: At Stage IX, Ov-ascl1 was expressed in the lateral lips surrounding the eye primordia. Expression could also be observed in retinal cells of the developing eyes and in the tissue delineating the mouth apparatus, and was absent from the cerebral, pedal, palliovisceral and optic cords (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4A

claim: At subsequent stages of organogenesis (XI, XIII, XV.2, and XVII), Ov-ascl1 was expressed in the lateral lips and was absent from the developing cords/brain lobes.
source: At subsequent stages of organogenesis (XI, XIII, XV.2, and XVII), Ov-ascl1 was expressed in the lateral lips and was absent from the developing cords/brain lobes (Figure 4B–E, low level staining that did not consistently appear in all replicates was considered background).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4B-E

claim: During maturation and right before hatching, the number of cells expressing Ov-ascl1 significantly decreased with the thinning lateral lips and transcripts were still absent from the optic lobes, supra- and subesophageal masses.
source: During maturation and right before hatching, the number of cells expressing Ov-ascl1 significantly decreased with the thinning lateral lips and transcripts were still absent from the optic lobes, supra- and subesophageal masses (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4F,G

claim: Ov-ngn transcripts were found in the lateral lips throughout organogenesis and maturation phases, while transcripts were absent from the developing brain cords.
source: In O. vulgaris embryos, we found Ov-ngn transcripts in the lateral lips throughout organogenesis and maturation phases, while transcripts were absent from the developing brain cords (Stage IX-XX.2, Figure 4H–N, Figure 4—figure supplement 6, low level staining that did not consistently appear in all replicates was considered background).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4H-N and Figure 4—figure supplement 6

claim: Very few Ov-ngn transcripts were present in both transition zones at Stages XIII to XX.2.
source: In addition, very few Ov-ngn transcripts were present in both transition zones at Stages XIII to XX.2 (Figure 4J–N).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4J-N

claim: The number of Ov-ngn expressing cells decreased considerably in the maturation phase with the thinning of the lateral lips and at Stage XX.2, only few cells were expressing Ov-ngn.
source: Equivalent to Ov-ascl1, the number of Ov-ngn expressing cells decreased considerably in the maturation phase with the thinning of the lateral lips and at Stage XX.2, only few cells were expressing Ov-ngn (Figure 4M,N).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4M,N

claim: Expression of both Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn consistently marks the proliferative lateral lips, with Ov-ascl1 expressing cells being more numerous compared to Ov-ngn expressing cells.
source: In summary, expression of both Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn consistently marks the proliferative lateral lips, with Ov-ascl1 expressing cells being more numerous compared to Ov-ngn expressing cells.
evidence: Summary inference based on Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn expression patterns

claim: At the beginning of organogenesis (Stage IX and XI), Ov-neuroD was expressed in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal and optic cords of the central nervous system.
source: At the beginning of organogenesis (Stage IX and XI), Ov-neuroD was expressed in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal and optic cords of the central nervous system.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization observations

claim: At Stage IX and XI, Ov-neuroD transcripts were detected in the lateral lips, although in fewer cells compared to the cords.
source: Transcripts were also detected in the lateral lips, although in fewer cells compared to the cords (Figure 4O,P).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4O,P

claim: At Stage XI in the optic cords, a medio-lateral expression gradient of Ov-neuroD was observed with high expression at the medial side and low expression at the lateral side, closer to the eyes.
source: At Stage XI in the optic cords, a medio-lateral expression gradient was observed with high Ov-neuroD at the medial side and low Ov-neuroD at the lateral side, closer to the eyes.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization observations

claim: At Stage XI, Ov-neuroD seemed more highly expressed in the cerebral and palliovisceral cords compared to the pedal cord.
source: Ov-neuroD also seemed more highly expressed in the cerebral and palliovisceral cords compared to the pedal cord (Figure 4P).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4P

claim: At Stage XIII, Ov-neuroD transcripts were absent from the region of Ov-ascl1 expressing cells in the lateral lips, but were present adjacent to those cells on the posterior side of the embryo next to the sinus ophthalmicus, marking the posterior transition zone.
source: At Stage XIII, Ov-neuroD transcripts were absent from the region of Ov-ascl1 expressing cells in the lateral lips, but were present adjacent to those cells on the posterior side of the embryo next to the sinus ophthalmicus, and mark the posterior transition zone.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization observations

claim: At Stage XIII, Ov-neuroD expression in the cerebral, palliovisceral and optic cords was significantly reduced compared to earlier stages and expression in the pedal cord was elevated.
source: In addition, Ov-neuroD expression in the cerebral, palliovisceral and optic cords was significantly reduced compared to earlier stages and expression in the pedal cord was elevated (Figure 4Q).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4Q

claim: At Stages XV.2 and XVII, high level Ov-neuroD expression marked both the anterior and posterior transition zones.
source: At Stages XV.2 and XVII, high level Ov-neuroD expression marked both the anterior and posterior transition zones.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization observations

claim: At Stages XV.2 and XVII, Ov-neuroD transcripts were present at low level in the optic lobes on the medial side, and in the outer layers of the supra- and subesophageal masses.
source: In the central brain, transcripts were present at low level in the optic lobes on the medial side, and in the outer layers of the supra- and subesophageal masses (Figure 4R,S, low level staining in the developing cords/lobes that did not consistently appear in all replicates was considered background).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4R,S

claim: At Stages XIX.1 and XX.2, Ov-neuroD showed clear expression in the transition zones.
source: A similar expression pattern was visible at Stages XIX.1 and XX.2 with clear expression in the transition zones (Figure 4T,U).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4T,U

claim: Ov-neuroD transcripts label the transition zones that connect the proliferative lateral lips to the postmitotic central brain.
source: Ov-neuroD transcripts thus label the transition zones that connect the proliferative lateral lips to the postmitotic central brain.
evidence: Summary inference based on Ov-neuroD expression pattern

claim: Ov-ngn and Ov-ascl1 are likely expressed in a different subset of progenitor cells, since their expression was not overlapping.
source: In a hybridization chain reaction experiment combined with immunohistochemistry, we show that Ov-ngn and Ov-ascl1 are likely expressed in a different subset of progenitor cells, since their expression was not overlapping (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Based on HCR experiment shown in Figure 5A-C

claim: Ov-ascl1+ progenitor cells seem more proliferative compared to Ov-ngn+ progenitors, that rarely overlap with the PH3+ population at late-organogenesis stage.
source: Furthermore, co-staining with the PH3 antibody demonstrated that Ov-ascl1+ progenitor cells seem more proliferative compared to Ov-ngn+ progenitors, that rarely overlap with the PH3+ population at this late-organogenesis stage (Figure 5A–G).
evidence: Based on HCR combined with immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5A-G

claim: The proximity of Ov-ngn+ cells to dividing Ov-ascl1+ progenitors could be a sign of asymmetric progenitor division during neurogenesis in octopus.
source: The proximity of Ov-ngn+ cells to dividing Ov-ascl1+ progenitors could be a sign of asymmetric progenitor division during neurogenesis in octopus.
evidence: Speculative inference based on spatial relationship of cell types

claim: Ov-neuroD expressing cells did not co-localize with PH3 immunoreactive cells, indicating that Ov-neuroD is absent from mitotically active cells in octopus embryos, at least at Stage XV.2.
source: In addition, Ov-neuroD expressing cells did not co-localize with PH3 immunoreactive cells, indicating that Ov-neuroD is absent from mitotically active cells in octopus embryos, at least at Stage XV.2 (Figure 5H–M).
evidence: Based on HCR combined with immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5H-M

claim: If the progenitor cells in the lateral lips would contribute neurons to the CNS, postmitotic neurons would need to travel long distances from the lateral lips to the central brain.
source: If the progenitor cells in the lateral lips identified in this study would contribute neurons to the CNS, postmitotic neurons would need to travel long distances from the lateral lips to the central brain.
evidence: Logical inference based on anatomical distance between lateral lips and central brain

claim: At hatching, the major lobes described for the adult supra- and subesophageal masses can be distinguished.
source: At hatching, the major lobes described for the adult supra- and subesophageal masses can be distinguished, with the supraesophageal mass consisting of buccal, inferior frontal, superior frontal, subfrontal, vertical, subvertical, basal, dorsal basal and medial basal lobes, and the subesophageal mass consisting of the palliovisceral and pedal lobes (Figure 6A–C; Young, 1971).
evidence: Based on anatomical observations shown in Figure 6A-C; supported by citation to Young, 1971

claim: Progenitor cells in the lateral lips generate output to the different lobes in the supra- and subesophageal masses.
source: For these regions, we identified progenitor cells in the lateral lips that generate output to the different lobes in the supra- and subesophageal masses (Figure 6D–J).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 6D-J

claim: A major contribution to the palliovisceral lobe found its origin in progenitor cells in the dorsal-posterior quadrant of the lateral lips at Stage IX.
source: Specifically, a major contribution to the palliovisceral lobe found its origin in progenitor cells in the dorsal-posterior quadrant of the lateral lips at Stage IX, as was suggested but not empirically proven by Koenig et al., 2016 (example in Figure 6D–E).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6D-E; supported by citation to Koenig et al., 2016

claim: Progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lip distinctly contributed cells to the inferior and superior frontal lobes of the supraesophageal mass at all stages.
source: In addition, progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lip distinctly contributed cells to the inferior and superior frontal lobes of the supraesophageal mass at all stages, which has not been reported before by Koenig et al., 2016 (example in Figure 6G–H).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6G-H; comparison to Koenig et al., 2016

claim: Progenitor cells in the ventral lateral lips produced cells destined to the basal lobes (basal lobe, dorsal basal lobe, medial basal lobe) of the supraesophageal mass.
source: Progenitor cells in the ventral lateral lips also produced cells destined to the basal lobes (basal lobe, dorsal basal lobe, medial basal lobe) of the supraesophageal mass (orange and red injection spots in Figure 6D,G,I).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6D,G,I

claim: The majority of cells located in the supraesophageal mass were derived from ventral-anterior progenitor cells in the lateral lips.
source: The majority of cells located in the supraesophageal mass, however, were derived from ventral-anterior progenitor cells in the lateral lips (example in Figure 6D,F,I,J).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6D,F,I,J

claim: Few labeled progenitor populations generated cells for the pedal lobe of the subesophageal mass.
source: In contrast to the supraesophageal mass and the palliovisceral lobe, few labeled progenitor populations generated cells for the pedal lobe of the subesophageal mass.
evidence: Based on lineage tracing observations

claim: Ventral-anterior progenitor populations at Stage XV.2 generated cells for the pedal lobe.
source: Apart from the ventral-anterior progenitor populations at Stage XV.2 (example in Figure 6I–J), we did not identify progenitor populations that gave rise to a significant number of cells that migrated to the pedal lobe.
evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6I-J

claim: Progenitor cells in the dorsal-anterior quadrant of the lateral lips gave rise to cells in the optic lobes, for which labeled cells generally located to the inner and outer granular layers of the cortex.
source: Focusing on the output to the optic lobe and peduncle complex (Figure 7), we identified progenitor cells in the dorsal-anterior quadrant of the lateral lips that gave rise to cells in the optic lobes, for which labeled cells generally located to the inner and outer granular layers of the cortex (black populations with an asterisk in Figure 7A,C,E; example of progeny in Figure 7D).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 7A,C,E,D

claim: Progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lips at Stages IX and XII.1 generated optic lobe cells that resided in the medulla.
source: Progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lips at Stages IX and XII.1 generated optic lobe cells that resided in the medulla, while at Stage XV.2, more cells located to the optic lobe cortex as well (example in Figure 7A,B,E,F).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 7A,B,E,F

claim: At Stage XV.2, progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lips generated more cells that located to the optic lobe cortex.
source: Progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lips at Stages IX and XII.1 generated optic lobe cells that resided in the medulla, while at Stage XV.2, more cells located to the optic lobe cortex as well (example in Figure 7A,B,E,F).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 7A,B,E,F

claim: Ventral-anterior lateral lip progenitors did not generate optic lobe cells.
source: Ventral-anterior lateral lip progenitors did not generate optic lobe cells.
evidence: Based on lineage tracing observations

claim: Progenitors in the posterior and ventral lateral lips generated cells destined to the peduncle complex (olfactory and peduncle lobe).
source: We also identified a clear spatial patterning of progenitors that generate cells for the peduncle complex (olfactory and peduncle lobe). Progenitors in the posterior and ventral lateral lips generated cells destined to this complex (example in Figure 7A–B), while populations on the dorsal-anterior side did not.
evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 7A-B

claim: Populations on the dorsal-anterior side of the lateral lips did not generate cells for the peduncle complex.
source: We also identified a clear spatial patterning of progenitors that generate cells for the peduncle complex (olfactory and peduncle lobe). Progenitors in the posterior and ventral lateral lips generated cells destined to this complex (example in Figure 7A–B), while populations on the dorsal-anterior side did not.
evidence: Based on lineage tracing observations

claim: The lineage tracing study identified spatial and temporal patterning in the lateral lips, which generate neurons for specific brain regions.
source: Taken together, our lineage tracing study identified spatial and temporal patterning in the lateral lips, which generate neurons for specific brain regions.
evidence: Summary inference based on lineage tracing experiments

claim: Labeled cells in the lateral lips divided and migrated posteriorly and entered the posterior transition zone.
source: Labeled cells in the lateral lips (intense labeling, Figure 8G–L) divided and migrated posteriorly and entered the posterior transition zone (labeling intensity decreased, Figure 8D–F).
evidence: Based on short-term lineage tracing shown in Figure 8D-L

claim: Cells could be traced towards the ventral side of the embryo in the posterior transition zone after which they occupied all layers in the optic lobe.
source: Then, cells could be traced towards the ventral side of the embryo in the posterior transition zone (Figure 8F–P) after which they occupied all layers in the optic lobe (Figure 8G–R).
evidence: Based on short-term lineage tracing shown in Figure 8F-R

claim: Forty-eight hr tracing combined with HCR showed migrating cells in the posterior transition zone that expressed Ov-neuroD and low-level Ov-elav, indicative of newly formed neurons.
source: Forty-eight hr tracing combined with HCR on thin sections showed migrating cells in the posterior transition zone that expressed Ov-neuroD and low-level Ov-elav, indicative of newly formed neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing combined with HCR shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-D

claim: The first cells that reached the optic lobe expressed Ov-elav, confirming their neuronal identity.
source: The first cells that reached the optic lobe expressed Ov-elav, confirming their neuronal identity (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B,E).
evidence: Based on lineage tracing combined with HCR shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B,E

claim: Populations labeled at different locations in the lateral lips showed similar trajectories, with cells passing the dorsal and posterior lateral lips before entering the posterior transition zone and then the optic lobe.
source: Populations labeled at a different location in the lateral lips showed similar trajectories (even the most anterior labeled population in Figure 8—figure supplement 1), with cells passing the dorsal and posterior lateral lips before entering the posterior transition zone and then the optic lobe.
evidence: Based on multiple lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: Cells destined for the optic lobe seem to take a defined path via the posterior transition zone.
source: Taken together, cells destined for the optic lobe seem to take a defined path via the posterior transition zone.
evidence: Summary inference based on trajectory mapping experiments

claim: The embryonic octopus brain is practically devoid of dividing cells from Stage XI onwards.
source: This study showed that the embryonic octopus brain is practically devoid of dividing cells from Stage XI onwards.
evidence: Summary of findings from Ov-pcna and PH3 data

claim: A transient embryonic structure surrounding the developing eye – the lateral lips – harbors proliferative cells expressing conserved pro-neural transcription factors.
source: Instead, we identified a transient embryonic structure surrounding the developing eye – the lateral lips – that harbors proliferative cells expressing conserved pro-neural transcription factors.
evidence: Summary of findings from Ov-pcna, PH3, Ov-ascl1, and Ov-ngn data

claim: The spatiotemporal expression patterns of neurogenic genes suggest their involvement in regulating the development of the CNS in O. vulgaris.
source: The spatiotemporal expression patterns of these neurogenic genes suggest their involvement in regulating the development of the CNS in O. vulgaris.
evidence: Inference based on expression patterns of multiple neurogenic genes

claim: Koenig et al. have suggested a basic fate map of the neural primordia in D. pealeii using DiI tracing experiments, and identified contributions of cells from the lateral lips to the developing central brain.
source: Koenig et al. have suggested a basic fate map of the neural primordia in D. pealeii using DiI tracing experiments, and identified contributions of cells from the lateral lips to the developing central brain (Koenig et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koenig et al., 2016

claim: The spatial map of progenitor contributions seems to be conserved in cephalopods.
source: Our data using a carboxyfluorescein ester that is less leaky compared to DiI, indicate that the spatial map seems to be conserved in cephalopods.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of lineage tracing results in O. vulgaris with D. pealeii

claim: Patterning in the lateral lips is established at early neurogenesis stages and is grossly temporally maintained, suggesting that lobe-specificity is determined early on within the progenitor area.
source: In addition, we show that patterning is established at early neurogenesis stages and is grossly temporally maintained, suggesting that lobe-specificity is determined early on within the progenitor area.
evidence: Inference based on lineage tracing at different developmental stages

claim: Long-distance migration of cells generated in the lateral lips towards the central brain occurs in octopuses.
source: Next to clear spatial patterning in the lateral lips, we identified long-distance migration of cells generated in the lateral lips towards the central brain in octopuses.
evidence: Based on lineage tracing and trajectory mapping experiments

claim: In O. bimaculoides, Ov-elav expression was already reported from Stage VII.2 onwards, pointing toward rapid neuronal differentiation.
source: In O. bimaculoides, expression was already reported from Stage VII.2 onwards, pointing toward rapid neuronal differentiation (Shigeno et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shigeno et al., 2015

claim: In S. officinalis, Sof-elav1 expression is unequally distributed over the different cords, and disappears toward the end of embryonic development, pointing to a different timing of neuronal differentiation and a more advanced maturation of the Sepia brain at hatching.
source: In contrast to both octopus species, Sof-elav1 expression in the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis is unequally distributed over the different cords, and disappears toward the end of embryonic development, pointing to a different timing of neuronal differentiation and a more advanced maturation of the Sepia brain at hatching (Buresi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buresi et al., 2013; inference about maturation timing

claim: S. officinalis embryos have been described to respond to tactile and chemical as well as visual cues from within the egg capsule from Stage XV.1 and XVI onwards, respectively.
source: Consistent with this, S. officinalis embryos have been described to respond to tactile and chemical as well as visual cues from within the egg capsule from Stage XV.1 and XVI onwards, respectively (Romagny et al., 2012) (for interspecies stage comparison, see Deryckere et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Romagny et al., 2012 and Deryckere et al., 2020

claim: O. vulgaris embryos only seem to react to visual stimuli (chromatophore contraction in response to light change) and mechanical stimuli (mantle contraction after tapping the chorion) from Stage XIX.1 onwards.
source: In our hands, O. vulgaris embryos only seem to react to visual stimuli (chromatophore contraction in response to light change) and mechanical stimuli (mantle contraction after tapping the chorion) from Stage XIX.1 onwards (preliminary observation).
evidence: Based on preliminary observations by the authors

claim: Neural processes visualized with immunostaining against acetylated alpha-tubulin revealed the presence of neurites in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal, and optic cords of O. bimaculoides and S. officinalis embryos as early as Stage VIII.
source: Furthermore, neural processes visualized with immunostaining against acetylated alpha-tubulin revealed the presence of neurites in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal, and optic cords of O. bimaculoides and S. officinalis embryos as early as Stage VIII, while we only observed expression of Ov-syt and presence of acetylated alpha-tubulin in the central brain from Stages XIII and XV.2 onwards, respectively (Baratte and Bonnaud, 2009; Shigeno et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baratte and Bonnaud, 2009; Shigeno et al., 2015

claim: These findings support the delayed maturation of the brain in O. vulgaris, that perhaps uses its paralarval phase to complete maturation of the nervous system.
source: These findings further support the delayed maturation of the brain in O. vulgaris, that perhaps uses its paralarval phase to complete maturation of the nervous system.
evidence: Inference based on comparative developmental timing; speculation about paralarval maturation

claim: Ov-soxB1 expression is not restricted to neurectodermal progenitor regions.
source: Ov-soxB1 expression is not restricted to neurectodermal progenitor regions.
evidence: Based on Ov-soxB1 expression pattern observations

claim: Consistent with Sof-soxB1 expression in S. officinalis, Ov-soxB1 is expressed at high level in the surface ectoderm, in the developing eyes, and is absent from the gills and stellate ganglia.
source: Consistent with Sof-soxB1 expression in S. officinalis, Ov-soxB1 is expressed at high level in the surface ectoderm, in the developing eyes, and is absent from the gills and stellate ganglia (Focareta and Cole, 2016).
evidence: Based on Ov-soxB1 expression observations; supported by citation to Focareta and Cole, 2016

claim: soxB1 is expressed in sensory epithelia in vertebrates, invertebrate mollusks and acoelomate worms.
source: Next to (neur)ectodermal expression, soxB1 is also expressed in sensory epithelia in vertebrates, invertebrate mollusks and acoelomate worms (Focareta and Cole, 2016; Guo et al., 2010; Kiernan et al., 2005; Le Gouar et al., 2004; Neves et al., 2007; Semmler et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: SOXB1 proteins are present in both neurectodermal stem cells and differentiated neurons in certain species.
source: In addition, SOXB1 proteins are present in both neurectodermal stem cells and differentiated neurons in certain species.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about SOXB1 function

claim: Drosophila soxN and Schmidtea polychroa soxB1 are expressed in early specification events in the CNS, but also in differentiated parts where they are involved in neuronal differentiation and axonal patterning, suggesting a dual role for protostome soxB1.
source: Drosophila soxN and Schmidtea polychroa soxB1 for example are expressed in early specification events in the CNS, but also in differentiated parts where they are involved in neuronal differentiation and axonal patterning, suggesting a dual role for protostome soxB1 (Ferrero et al., 2014; Girard et al., 2006; Monjo and Romero, 2015; Phochanukul and Russell, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferrero et al., 2014; Girard et al., 2006; Monjo and Romero, 2015; Phochanukul and Russell, 2010

claim: Some subtypes of (inter)neurons require SOXB1 proteins for proper specification and migration in vertebrates.
source: While such a general function in neuronal differentiation of vertebrate soxB1 factors has not been shown, some subtypes of (inter)neurons do require SOXB1 proteins for proper specification and migration (Cavallaro et al., 2008; Ekonomou et al., 2005; Panayi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cavallaro et al., 2008; Ekonomou et al., 2005; Panayi et al., 2010

claim: Expression data suggest a dual role for Ov-soxB1, in early nervous system development to specify neural fate, and later on to steer neural cell differentiation.
source: Similar to many other species, our expression data suggest a dual role for Ov-soxB1, in early nervous system development to specify neural fate, and later on to steer neural cell differentiation.
evidence: Inference based on Ov-soxB1 expression pattern; comparison to other species

claim: The expression pattern of Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn suggests the presence of a neurogenic domain in the lateral lips, outside the cords of the central brain.
source: Our study is the first one mapping the expression of ascl1 in cephalopods and together with the expression pattern of Ov-ngn, suggests the presence of a neurogenic domain in the lateral lips, outside the cords of the central brain (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: Inference based on Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn expression patterns shown in Figure 9A,B

claim: In the annelids Capitella teleta and P. dumerilii, neurogenin and ash1 are both expressed in actively proliferating neural progenitor cells in the neurectoderm.
source: In the annelids Capitella teleta and P. dumerilii, neurogenin and ash1 are both expressed in actively proliferating neural progenitor cells in the neurectoderm (Figure 9C).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge; shown in Figure 9C

claim: In C. teleta, Ct-ngn positive cells stay on the apical side, while Ct-ash1-positive progenitors ingress and undergo limited division before becoming Ct-elav positive.
source: While Ct-ngn positive cells stay on the apical side, the Ct-ash1-positive progenitors ingress and undergo limited division before becoming Ct-elav positive (Demilly et al., 2013; Meyer and Seaver, 2009; Simionato et al., 2008; Sur et al., 2017; Sur et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Demilly et al., 2013; Meyer and Seaver, 2009; Simionato et al., 2008; Sur et al., 2017; Sur et al., 2020

claim: In O. vulgaris, the Ov-ascl1 progenitor population seems to be more proliferative compared to the Ov-ngn progenitor population, at least at Stage XV.2 (late organogenesis), which suggests their sequential expression could be turned around in cephalopods.
source: In O. vulgaris, the Ov-ascl1 progenitor population seems to be more proliferative compared to the Ov-ngn progenitor population, at least at Stage XV.2 (late organogenesis), which suggests their sequential expression could be turned around in cephalopods (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: Based on HCR data shown in Figure 9B,C; inference about sequential expression

claim: The Ov-elav expressing neurons in the cords are not located immediately basal from the Ov-ascl1 or Ov-ngn positive pool of neural progenitor cells.
source: In addition, the Ov-elav expressing neurons in the cords are not located immediately basal from the Ov-ascl1 or Ov-ngn positive pool of neural progenitor cells.
evidence: Based on spatial relationship of expression domains

claim: A population of Ov-neuroD expressing cells is found in the transition zones, in between the Ov-ascl1+ and Ov-ngn+ lateral lips and the developing Ov-elav+ brain, suggesting an intermediate, Ov-neuroD+ population is present in O. vulgaris.
source: In particular, a population of Ov-neuroD expressing cells is found in the transition zones, in between the Ov-ascl1+ and Ov-ngn+ lateral lips and the developing Ov-elav+ brain, suggesting an intermediate, Ov-neuroD+ population is present in O. vulgaris (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: Based on Ov-neuroD expression pattern shown in Figure 9A,B; inference about intermediate population

claim: neuroD genes are lost in Drosophila and Ciona intestinalis.
source: While lost in Drosophila and Ciona intestinalis, neuroD genes can be widely found in bilaterians, where they steer the differentiation of neurons (Ledent et al., 2002; Stollewerk and Simpson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ledent et al., 2002; Stollewerk and Simpson, 2005

claim: neuroD genes can be widely found in bilaterians, where they steer the differentiation of neurons.
source: While lost in Drosophila and Ciona intestinalis, neuroD genes can be widely found in bilaterians, where they steer the differentiation of neurons (Ledent et al., 2002; Stollewerk and Simpson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ledent et al., 2002; Stollewerk and Simpson, 2005

claim: In the trunk of the annelid P. dumerilii (but not C. teleta) and in the developing nervous system of the planaria S. polychroa and S. mediterranea, neuroD seems broadly expressed in the neurectoderm, which suggests that the role of neuroD might not be conserved in Spiralia.
source: In contrast, in the trunk of the annelid P. dumerilii (but not C. teleta) and in the developing nervous system of the planaria S. polychroa and S. mediterranea, neuroD seems broadly expressed in the neurectoderm, which suggests that the role of neuroD might not be conserved in Spiralia (Figure 9C; Cowles et al., 2013; Meyer and Seaver, 2009; Monjo and Romero, 2015; Simionato et al., 2008; Sur et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cowles et al., 2013; Meyer and Seaver, 2009; Monjo and Romero, 2015; Simionato et al., 2008; Sur et al., 2020; shown in Figure 9C

claim: In vertebrates, ascl1 and ngn are expressed in a complementary fashion, both exerting proneuronal functions in neurogenesis.
source: In vertebrates, ascl1 and ngn are expressed in a complementary fashion, both exerting proneuronal functions in neurogenesis (Bertrand et al., 2002; Castro et al., 2011; Farah et al., 2000; Gradwohl et al., 1996; Lee et al., 1995; Ma et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertrand et al., 2002; Castro et al., 2011; Farah et al., 2000; Gradwohl et al., 1996; Lee et al., 1995; Ma et al., 1996

claim: Similar to data in octopus, neurogenin expression precedes, but also partially overlaps with that of neuroD in vertebrates.
source: Similar to our data in octopus, neurogenin expression precedes, but also partially overlaps with that of neuroD (Grimaldi et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grimaldi et al., 2008; comparison to octopus data

claim: Drosophila has only one neurogenin/neuroD homolog called tap, which relates better to neurogenin based on sequence similarities, but does not have a proneural role and is expressed in a few neurons, regulating their differentiation, axonal growth and guidance.
source: In contrast, Drosophila has only one neurogenin/neuroD homolog called tap, which relates better to neurogenin based on sequence similarities, but does not have a proneural role and is expressed in a few neurons, regulating their differentiation, axonal growth and guidance (Gautier et al., 1997; Vervoort and Ledent, 2001; Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gautier et al., 1997; Vervoort and Ledent, 2001; Yuan et al., 2016

claim: In arthropods, the members of the achaete-scute subfamily are expressed in proneural clusters and promote the generation of neural progenitor cells from quiescent ectodermal cells.
